intro.carita: Uttama Carita (the third episode, chapters 5–13), of which this is the second and last of the two battles with the asura brothers. In the recitation tradition its presiding form is Mahāsarasvatī; this is the Gita Press viniyoga (printed before chapter 5), not a statement of the Purāṇa text. In the Gita Press pāṭha chapter 10 has no viniyoga of its own, only a dhyāna, of Kāmeśvarī: bright as heated gold, with the sun, moon and fire for her eyes, holding in her lovely arms the bow with arrows, the goad, the noose and the trident, the form of Śiva and Śakti (शिवशक्तिरूपां), wearing the crescent moon. The dhyāna is liturgy; the chapter itself never names Kāmeśvarī.
intro.summary: Seeing his brother Niśumbha, dear to him as life, lying dead and his army being cut down, Śumbha taunts the Goddess: wicked Durgā, puffed up with pride, she fights by leaning on the strength of others (10.1–3). She answers that she is alone in the world, and that there is no second beside her; the goddesses he sees are her own powers, and they are entering her as he watches (10.4–5). Brahmāṇī and the others dissolve into her body, and Ambikā stands alone (10.6). She tells him that she had stood there in many forms through her power, has withdrawn them, and now faces him alone: let him stand firm (10.7–8). The duel begins before the watching gods and asuras (10.9–11). Śumbha breaks her divine missiles with counter-weapons; she breaks his as if in play, with a fierce cry of ‘huṃ’ and the like (10.12–13). One by one she cuts away his bow, his spear, his sword and shield, and his mace; he has lost his horses and his charioteer, and comes on with his bare fist (10.14–19). His blow lands on her heart; the flat of her hand fells him, and he is up again at once (10.20–21). He seizes her and rises into the sky, where she fights without any support, and the two wrestle there, to the wonder of the siddhas and sages (10.22–23). She lifts him, whirls him round and hurls him to earth; he charges once more, fist raised, and she pierces his chest with her trident (10.24–26). He falls lifeless, and the whole earth shakes, with its oceans, continents and mountains (10.27). With him dead, the world grows clear and whole again: the sky clears, the portents vanish, the rivers keep their courses, the gods rejoice, the gandharvas sing, the apsarases dance, pure winds blow, the sun shines, the fires burn calm and the noise of the quarters is stilled (10.28–32).
intro.forms: The Devī, through the narrative and the duel (10.6, 10.10, 10.14–16, 10.20, 10.26–27); Durgā, the name Śumbha uses in his taunt (10.3); Ambikā, ‘Mother’, as she stands alone and as she fights (10.6, 10.12, 10.18, 10.24); Caṇḍikā, ‘the fierce one’, in the close fight (10.17, 10.22–23, 10.25); and Parameśvarī, ‘the supreme sovereign’, as she breaks his missiles in play (10.13). The Mothers, ‘Brahmāṇī and the rest’ (10.6), appear only to disappear: she calls them her own vibhūtis, powers (10.5), and her many forms, assumed through her power (10.8), and draws them back into herself.
intro.significance: The chapter is named for the second brother’s death (colophon: शुम्भवधः), and with it the battles of the Devī Māhātmya end. Its centre is not the duel but the exchange before it. Śumbha’s charge, that she fights by the strength of others (10.3), is answered by the claim ‘I alone am here in the world’ (10.5), and the narrative makes the claim visible: the Mothers who fought in chapters 8–9 dissolve into her body, and Ambikā stands alone (10.6). The duel that follows takes from Śumbha his weapons one at a time (10.14–19), then the ground under him (10.22–24), then his life (10.26–27), and the chapter ends not with the victory but with its effect on the world: the clearing of sky, rivers, winds, sun and fires (10.28–32). Chapter 11, the gods’ hymn to Nārāyaṇī, follows.
intro.grammar: A battle narrative in the perfect again: reduplicated forms (मुमुचे, बभञ्ज, चिच्छेद, जग्राह, निपपात, युयुधे, चिक्षेप, पपात), a dual with two subjects joined by च (चक्रतुः, 10.23), the plural perfects of the rejoicing (बभूवुः, जगुः, ननृतुः, ववुः, जज्वलुः, 10.30–32) and the periphrastic perfect of causatives (पातयामास, 10.20, 10.26; भ्रामयामास, 10.24). Imperfects (अब्रवीत्, आच्छादयत, अभ्यधावत्/अभ्यधावत, अताडयत्, अवादयन्) and the aorist अभूत् (10.11, 10.31) stand beside them. Absolutes set the turns: a genitive absolute (पश्यतां सर्वदेवानाम्, 10.10) and locative absolutes (छिन्ने धनुषि, 10.15; हते तस्मिन् दुरात्मनि, 10.28; पातिते, 10.29; निहते तस्मिन्, 10.30). The dialogue gives a prohibition with मा and the imperative (मा … आवह, 10.3), a rhetorical question (द्वितीया का ममापरा, 10.5), present participles as predicates (विशन्त्यः, 10.5) and a past participle with an object (यद् आस्थिता, 10.8). Prefixed absolutives in -य run through the fight (उपादाय, उद्यम्य, प्रगृह्य, उत्पत्य, उत्पात्य, प्राप्य), and bahuvrīhis strip Śumbha of what he had (हताश्वः, छिन्नधन्वा, विसारथिः, 10.18; गतासुः, 10.27).
intro.teaching: Literally, the last asura king is killed in single combat, and the world, freed of him, returns to order. As teaching, the Śākta tradition reads 10.5–8 as the doctrinal heart of the third carita: the many goddesses are one Goddess, her manifestations are her own power and not another’s, and what she has put forth she can take back (संहृतम्, 10.8, the verb of cosmic withdrawal). Śumbha’s error is to see many where there is one (10.3). The duel that strips him of every means of attack, and the restoration of nature that follows his death (10.28–32), are read as the outward side of that truth; reading the fires of 10.32 as the sacrificial fires is traditional interpretation, and the commentary offers it as such. The chapter’s own words are narrative; the non-dual reading is the tradition’s, and it is presented that way.
themes: ‘I alone am here’: the many goddesses as one
The charge of borrowed strength, answered
The duel that strips the asura of everything
Lordship as play: the hum-sound and the open hand

conclusion.narrative: Śumbha, the last of the asura brothers, sees Niśumbha dead and accuses the Goddess of fighting on the strength of others. She answers that there is no one else: the goddesses who fought beside her are her own powers, and as she speaks they enter her body, and Ambikā stands alone. In single combat she breaks his missiles as if in play, cuts away his bow, spear, sword, shield and mace, fells him with the flat of her hand, fights him in the sky with nothing to stand on, throws him down and pierces him with her trident. He falls and the earth shakes; then the sky, the rivers, the winds, the sun and the fires return to their nature, and the gods rejoice. The battles of the text are over; chapter 11 is the gods’ hymn of thanks.

vocabulary.en: one, alone: the Goddess’s word for herself (एकैवाहम्, 10.5) and the narrator’s for her (10.6, 10.8)
a second (woman): ‘who else is there besides me?’ (10.5)
manifested power; the goddesses as her own powers (10.5, 10.8)
dissolution, merging back into the source (10.6)
drawn together, withdrawn: the verb of cosmic dissolution (10.8)
the cry ‘huṃ’, the Goddess’s sound used as a weapon (10.13)
without support; here, fighting in mid-air (10.22)
trident or spear: the weapon of the death blow (10.26–27)
health, soundness; lit. ‘being established in oneself’ (10.28)

constructions: The prohibitive मा with the imperative, the Epic and Purāṇic idiom (मा … गर्वम् आवह, 10.3).
A rhetorical question as a denial (द्वितीया का मम अपरा, 10.5), and a present participle as predicate after पश्य (पश्य एताः … विशन्त्यः, 10.5).

The genitive absolute of spectators (पश्यतां सर्वदेवानाम् असुराणां च, 10.10) and locative absolutes for each turn and for the aftermath (छिन्ने धनुषि, 10.15; हते तस्मिन् दुरात्मनि, 10.28; पातिते, 10.29).
The perfect dual with two subjects joined by च (दैत्यः चण्डिका च … चक्रतुः, 10.23).
The periphrastic perfect of causative stems (पातयामास, 10.20, 10.26; भ्रामयामास, 10.24) beside a string of absolutives (उत्पात्य भ्रामयामास चिक्षेप, 10.24).
Bahuvrīhis of loss (हताश्वः, छिन्नधन्वा, विसारथिः, 10.18; गतासुः, 10.27) and with स- for सह (साब्धिद्वीपां सपर्वताम्, 10.27; सोल्काः, 10.29).
Agent nouns in compounds that govern their object (तत्प्रतीघातकर्तृभिः, 10.12; सिद्धमुनिविस्मयकारकम्, 10.23).
One participle in two functions: शान्ताः qualifying the fires and then predicating the stillness of the sounds (10.32).
insights: The Goddess is one without a second: the powers that fought beside her are not others but her own vibhūtis, and they return into her (10.5–6).
Manifestation and withdrawal are both her act: what she assumed through her power in many forms she has drawn back (संहृतम्), and she stands alone (10.8).
The demon’s error is to see many where there is one; his taunt of borrowed strength (10.3) is answered not by argument but by the visible dissolution of the Mothers into her (10.6).
Her sovereignty acts as play: as Parameśvarī she breaks his divine missiles with a cry of ‘huṃ’, as if in sport (10.13), and fells him with the flat of her hand (10.20–21).
She depends on nothing: when Śumbha carries the fight into the sky she fights there without support (निराधारा, 10.22).
Her victory heals the world itself, not only the gods: sky, rivers, winds, sun and fires return to their nature when the asura falls (10.28–32).
conclusion.srividya: The chapter shares names and ideas with the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa). The Goddess’s claim to be alone (10.5) is stated there as names: एकाकिनी (665), निर्द्वैता (667) and द्वैतवर्जिता (668). The dissolution of the Mothers into her (10.6) recalls लयकरी (739); her breaking his missiles in play (10.13) recalls परमेश्वरी (396) and लीलाविनोदिनी (966); and निराधारा (132), a metaphysical name there, is a literal word here (10.22). The duel of weapon and counter-weapon (10.12) has its parallel in Lalitā’s war with Bhaṇḍāsura (79, भण्डासुरेन्द्रनिर्मुक्तशस्त्रप्रत्यस्त्रवर्षिणी), but the stories are different. The one specifically Śrīvidyā element is liturgical, not textual: the Gita Press dhyāna before this chapter meditates on Kāmeśvarī, the form of Śiva and Śakti (compare शिवशक्त्यैक्यरूपिणी, 999), holding the bow and arrows, the goad and the noose — the four weapons the Lalitā Sahasranāma gives Lalitā (8–11, रागस्वरूपपाशाढ्या, क्रोधाकाराङ्कुशोज्ज्वला, मनोरूपेक्षुकोदण्डा, पञ्चतन्मात्रसायका) — with a trident added. The chapter itself states no Śrīvidyā doctrine; these are shared Śākta names and images, not evidence that one text depends on the other.

key_verses.why: Śumbha’s taunt: wicked Durgā, proud of her power, fights leaning on the strength of others.
एकैवाहं जगत्यत्र — I alone am here in the world; who else is there besides me? These powers of mine are entering me.
Brahmāṇī and the other goddesses dissolve into her body, and Ambikā stands alone.
The many forms she had assumed through her power she has withdrawn; now she stands alone in battle — let him stand firm.
As Parameśvarī she breaks his divine missiles as if in play, with a fierce cry of ‘huṃ’ and the like.
Pierced by the point of her trident, Śumbha falls lifeless, and the whole earth shakes with its oceans, continents and mountains.
With the wicked one slain, the whole world grows serene and regains its health, and the sky becomes clear.

sandhi_patterns: Visarga sandhi is the commonest junction: -aḥ before voiced sounds → -o (स्थिरो भव, 10.8; ततो नियुद्धम्, 10.24), visarga → ś/s before c/t (दैत्यश्छिन्नधन्वा, 10.18; दैत्येन्द्रस्तथा, 10.15), r-visarga restored before voiced sounds (बहुभिरिह, 10.8; जग्मुरेकैव, 10.6), and -aḥ + a → -o’ (क्रुद्धोऽब्रवीत्, 10.2; सोऽसुरः, 10.14; सोऽभ्यधावत्, 10.19; सुप्रभोऽभूत्, 10.31).
सः drops its visarga before consonants, repeatedly in the duel (स तदा, 10.18; स मुष्टिम्, 10.20; स दैत्यराजः, 10.21; स क्षिप्तः, 10.25; स गतासुः, 10.27).

Final n → ṃs before t (प्रागासंस्ते, तथासंस्तत्र, 10.29; अवादयंस्तथैव, 10.31); final t → n before a nasal (चाभवन्नभः, 10.28) and voiced before voiced sounds (बलावलेपाद् दुष्टे, 10.3; अभूद्भूयः, 10.11; यदास्थिता, 10.8).

Vowel sandhi of every kind: vṛddhi (एकैवाहम्, पश्यैताः, 10.5; मयैकैव, 10.8), yaṇ (जगत्यत्र, 10.5; तिष्ठाम्याजौ, 10.8; दिव्यान्यस्त्राणि, 10.12), guṇa (लीलयैवोग्र-, 10.13; तलेनोरस्यताडयत्, 10.20; पपातोर्व्याम्, 10.27), savarṇa-dīrgha (ममापरा, 10.5; तेनाम्बिका, 10.24).
No declared hiatus in the chapter.
samasa: Bahuvrīhis of loss and of state (हताश्वः, छिन्नधन्वा, विसारथिः, 10.18; गतासुः, 10.27; दुष्टात्मा, 10.25; हर्षनिर्भरमानसाः, 10.30), including prādi bahuvrīhis (विसारथिः; निराधारा, 10.22; दुरात्मनि, 10.28) and bahuvrīhis with स- for सह (साब्धिद्वीपाम्, सपर्वताम्, 10.27; सोल्काः, 10.29).

Nested tatpuruṣas of intent and agency (अम्बिकानिधनोद्यतः, 10.18; चण्डिकानिधनेच्छया, 10.25; देवीशूलाग्रविक्षतः, 10.27; तलप्रहाराभिहतः, 10.21), and ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣas with an agent noun governing its object (तत्प्रतीघातकर्तृभिः, 10.12; सिद्धमुनिविस्मयकारकम्, 10.23).

Upapada tatpuruṣas (सर्वलोकभयङ्करम्, 10.11, with the inserted m; मार्गवाहिन्यः, 10.29; दिवाकरः, 10.31) and titles of the asura king (दैत्येन्द्रः, 10.12, 10.15; दैत्यराजः, 10.21; सर्वदैत्यजनेश्वरम्, 10.26).

Karmadhārayas of the Goddess and of portent (परमेश्वरी, 10.13; उत्पातमेघाः, a madhyama-pada-lopin karmadhāraya, 10.29), an upamāna-pūrvapada karmadhāraya (अर्ककरामलम्, 10.17), and a bahuvrīhi with आदि (उग्रहुङ्कारोच्चारणादिभिः, 10.13).
grammar_notes: युद्ध्यसे (10.3) is the ordinary युध्यसे of √युध् (divādi, ātmanepada); the doubled dh is the Gita Press orthography.
एताः (10.5) is nominative, agreeing with विशन्त्यः and मद्विभूतयः; after पश्य the clause is a direct exclamation.
यत् in 10.8 is taken as the relative object of आस्थिता with तत् as correlative; an adverbial यत् = यदा gives the same sense.
√धाव् appears in both padas: अभ्यधावत् (10.16, 10.19) and अभ्यधावत (10.25).
In the Gita Press text Śumbha’s loss of horses and charioteer is told only by the compounds of 10.18; the line found at 10.17 in other witnesses narrates it.
प्रथमम् (10.23) is read as an adjective of नियुद्धम्, ‘a fight never seen before’; ललितम् (10.30) is an adverb, ‘sweetly’.
The first शान्ताः of 10.32 is read as ‘(burning) calm’; ‘(the fires) that had been put out’ is the alternative.
themes: The one Goddess and her vibhūtis
The duel that strips the asura
The world restored after Śumbha’s death
uncertain: 10.11: तथास्त्रैश्चैव दारुणैः (Gita Press) / तथा चास्त्रैः सुदारुणैः (GRETIL, Freund) — Textual Verification Required; the sense is the same.
10.16: अभ्यधावत्तदा देवीं (Gita Press) / अभ्यधावत तां देवीं (GRETIL, Freund) — Textual Verification Required; the sense is the same.
10.17: GRETIL and Freund add a third line, अश्वांश्च पातयामास रथं सारथिना सह — a recension variant, not in the Gita Press text, whose colophon count agrees with the two-line form; not analysed.

Interpretive doubts, none about the reading itself, are flagged on 10.14 (तत्कुपिता as a compound or तत् ‘thereupon’) and 10.32 (the first शान्ताः: calm, or previously extinguished); 10.11, 10.16 and 10.17 carry the variants above.
